title: 9. Congruence of Triangles and Inequalities in a Triangle

q.t: Two triangles with three pairs of equal sides are congruent by:
q.e: Side-Side-Side: three fixed lengths can only form one triangle.

q.t: Two triangles with two pairs of equal sides and the included angles equal are congruent by:
q.e: Side-Angle-Side: the angle must be between the two sides.

q.t: Two triangles with two pairs of equal angles and the included sides equal are congruent by:
q.e: Angle-Side-Angle.

q.t: RHS congruence applies to:
q.e: Right angle, Hypotenuse, Side.

q.t: CPCT stands for:
q.e: Once triangles are congruent, their remaining matching parts are equal too.

q.t: In a triangle, angles opposite to equal sides are:
q.e: This is the isosceles triangle theorem.

q.t: In a triangle, the side opposite the larger angle is:
q.e: A wider angle opens onto a longer side.

q.t: The sum of any two sides of a triangle is:
q.e: The straight path between two points is the shortest; going via the third vertex is longer.

q.t: Which of these is NOT a congruence criterion?
q.e: Equal angles fix only the shape, not the size.

q.t: If △ABC ≅ △DEF, then BC equals:
q.e: The order of letters gives the matching: B ↔ E and C ↔ F.

q.t: In △ABC, AB = AC and ∠B = 50°. Find ∠A (in degrees).
△ABC ≅ △PQR, ∠A = 40° and ∠Q = 75°. Find ∠C (in degrees).
Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 5 cm. The third side must be less than:
q.e: It must be shorter than the other two together.

q.t: In △ABC, ∠A = 70° and ∠B = 60°. Which is the longest side?
q.e: The longest side faces the largest angle, ∠A.

q.t: In △ABC, ∠A = 70° and ∠B = 60°. Which is the shortest side?
q.e: ∠C = 50° is the smallest angle, and AB is opposite it.

q.t: Of all the line segments from a point to a line, the shortest is the:
q.e: Any other segment is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose leg is the perpendicular.

q.t: Two sides and a NON-included angle are equal in two triangles. Are they necessarily congruent?
q.e: SSA can give two different triangles, so it is not a criterion.

q.t: Two angles and a non-included side are equal in two triangles. They are congruent by:
q.e: The third angles must also be equal (angle sum), which turns it into ASA.

q.t: Two equilateral triangles are congruent if they have:
q.e: All angles are already 60°; only the size can differ.

q.t: In △PQR, PQ = PR and ∠P = 100°. Find ∠Q (in degrees).
q.e: The base angles share 80°.

q.t: In △ABC, AB = AC and ∠A = 50°. Find the exterior angle at C (in degrees).
q.e: ∠C = (180 − 50) ÷ 2 = 65°, so the exterior angle is 115°.

q.t: In △PQR, PQ = 5 cm, QR = 7 cm and PR = 9 cm. Which angle is the largest?
q.e: The largest angle faces the longest side, PR.

q.t: Two sides of a triangle are 8 cm and 13 cm. How many whole-number lengths (in cm) can the third side have?
q.k: len([c for c in range(1,40) if 13-8<c<13+8])
q.e: More than 5 and less than 21: the values 6 to 20.

q.t: In a right-angled triangle, the longest side is the:
q.e: It faces the largest angle, 90°.

q.t: In an isosceles triangle, the median to the base is also:
o: An altitude and an angle bisector
q.e: It splits the triangle into two congruent halves (SSS).

q.t: In △ABC, AD is perpendicular to BC and bisects BC. Then AB = AC by congruence rule:
q.e: BD = DC, ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°, AD common.

q.t: The difference of any two sides of a triangle is:
q.e: This follows from a + c > b, which rearranges to a > b − c.

q.t: In △ABC, AB > AC. Then:
q.e: The angle opposite the longer side is larger: ∠C faces AB.

q.t: A triangle has sides x, x + 2 and 10 cm, where 10 cm is the longest. What is the smallest whole-number value of x?
q.k: min(x for x in range(1,20) if x+x+2>10)
q.e: x + (x + 2) > 10 gives x > 4.

q.t: In △ABC, ∠B = ∠C = 55°, AB = (2x + 3) cm and AC = (5x − 9) cm. Find AB (in cm).
q.e: Equal angles face equal sides: 2x + 3 = 5x − 9, so x = 4.

q.t: AD is a median of △ABC. Which statement is always true?
q.e: Extend AD its own length to E. Then ABEC is a parallelogram, and in △ABE: AB + BE > AE, i.e. AB + AC > 2AD.

q.t: An isosceles triangle has equal sides 10 cm and base 12 cm. Find its altitude to the base (in cm).
q.e: The altitude bisects the base: 10² − 6² = 64.

q.t: In quadrilateral ABCD, the perimeter is:
o: Greater than the sum of the diagonals
Equal to the sum of the diagonals
Less than the sum of the diagonals
q.e: Apply the triangle inequality in the four triangles made by the diagonals and add: 2 × perimeter > 2(AC + BD).

q.t: O is a point inside △ABC. Then OA + OB + OC is:
q.e: OA + OB > AB, OB + OC > BC, OC + OA > CA. Adding: 2(OA + OB + OC) > perimeter.

q.t: In △ABC, AB = AC and ∠B = 2∠A. Find ∠A (in degrees).
In △ABC, ∠A > ∠B > ∠C. Arrange the sides from longest to shortest.
q.e: BC faces ∠A (largest), AC faces ∠B and AB faces ∠C (smallest).

q.t: Two altitudes of a triangle are equal. The triangle must be:
q.e: The two right triangles sharing the base are congruent (RHS/AAS), which makes two sides equal.

q.t: The perimeter of a triangle is:
o: Greater than the sum of its three medians
Equal to the sum of its medians
Less than the sum of its medians
Half the sum of its medians
q.e: Each median is less than half the sum of the two sides from its vertex; adding the three results gives the claim.

q.t: In right △ABC, ∠B = 90° and AB = BC. Find ∠A (in degrees).
q.e: Equal sides face equal angles, and the two acute angles share 90°.

q.t: D is a point on side BC of △ABC such that AD = AC. Then:
q.e: ∠ADC = ∠C (isosceles △ADC). ∠ADC is an exterior angle of △ABD, so it exceeds ∠B. Hence ∠C > ∠B and AB > AC = AD.
